🇲🇽📚 <u>Free High School, Online, at Any Age: Prepa en Línea Opens Registration</u>

Mexico's Education Ministry opened registration for Prepa en Línea, its free online high school, from October 19 to 28. Education Secretary Mario Delgado announced it at the presidential press conference. The diploma has official validity and there is no age limit. Mexicans can apply whether they live in Mexico or abroad, and so can foreigners with legal residence. The only requirement is a finished secondary education. The program takes at least two years, across 16 submodules. Enrollment in the Bachillerato Nacional Margarita Maza also remains open.
banner: FREE ONLINE HIGH SCHOOL, ANY AGE

🇲🇽🧵 <u>The Women Who Embroider Mexico Earn Half What Men Do</u>

Women are more than 78% of Mexico's textile-artisan workforce, yet they earn about 3,700 pesos a month against roughly 7,400 for men, according to the report Tejiendo el cambio by UNIDAS, a women's fair-work network, based on INEGI's employment survey for late 2025. 96.6% of these women work informally and only 2.4% have social security. Crafts generate 18.4% of the cultural sector's GDP and 30.2% of its jobs (INEGI, 2024).

The report calls the copying of community designs without credit or fair pay "cultural extractivism" and sends recommendations to the Labor Ministry, IMSS, the Women's Ministry and Fonart. A blouse takes Blanca Arely, an embroiderer from Ocosingo, Chiapas, seven to ten days of work. Her demand: "A fair price. A fair retribution."
banner: ARTISANS: WOMEN EARN HALF OF MEN

🇲🇽🌾 <u>Agriculture Secretary: Mexican Farming Is Not Collapsing</u>

Agriculture Secretary Julio Berdegué and Marco L. Ramírez answer the "collapse" narrative in La Jornada with production numbers. At the end of López Obrador's term, Mexico had 20 million hectares under cultivation producing 521.8 million tons of food, worth 888.4 billion pesos in 2025 values. Against 1994, the year NAFTA took effect, that is 111% more food and 61% more production value.

They acknowledge that specific sectors face serious challenges. The national totals still show growth.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Mexico Demands the OAS Explain Why Allende's Portrait Vanished</u>

Mexico has asked the OAS General Secretariat to explain why Salvador Allende's portrait was taken down from the organization's Washington headquarters. The portrait was hung in 2023 under a resolution approved by consensus with the backing of 32 states, and Gabriel Boric unveiled it for the 50th anniversary of Pinochet's coup. Mexico first asked on October 6, got no answer, and is now taking the matter to the Permanent Council. It wants to know why the portrait was removed, where it is now, and whether it will be put back.

Allende died defending La Moneda on September 11, 1973. Mexico took in his widow, Hortensia Bussi, and thousands of Chilean exiles.
banner: ALLENDE PORTRAIT: MEXICO ASKS OAS WHY

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Mexico Is North America's Top Car Exporter</u>

From January to August 2026, Mexico exported $36.5 billion in cars, more than the US ($31.8 billion) or Canada ($17.8 billion), El Economista reports from national statistics data. All three fell: Mexico by 7.8%, the US by 13.4% and Canada by 9.9%. Since 2016, only Mexico has grown its car exports, from $31.4 billion to $59.4 billion in 2025, while US exports slid and Canada's fell 40%. China's exports, up 53% to $129 billion, now beat all of North America combined.
banner: CAR EXPORTS: MEXICO TOPS N. AMERICA

🇲🇽🚔 <u>Mexico City: High-Impact Crime Down 19% Under Brugada</u>

Security Secretary Pablo Vázquez told the Mexico City Congress that high-impact crime has fallen 19% under Clara Brugada. Homicides are down more than 18%, and the August and September 2026 levels "had not been seen in the last 20 years." Violent car theft is down 55%, and microbus passenger robberies are down 50%. Homicide convictions rose 18%, and police effectiveness reached a record 49.5% in public perception.

🇲🇽⚡ <u>CFE: 37% Fewer Blackouts, Power Back in 7 Hours Instead of 25</u>

From January to September 2026, power interruptions fell 37% compared with 2024, CFE director Emilia Calleja reported. Average restoration time dropped 72%, from 25 hours in 2025 to 7 hours in 2026. She credited new infrastructure in Querétaro, Baja California, Yucatán, San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Tabasco and Sinaloa. Work has also started on the Playacar–Chankanaab II undersea line to Cozumel. CFE reported accumulated revenues of 332.2 billion pesos through the second quarter.

🇲🇽🏠 <u>Mexico City Moves to Cap Rent Hikes at Inflation</u>

Clara Brugada presented the Law of Tenant Relations and Fair Rents. Under it, rents in Mexico City could not rise faster than annual inflation, but they would not be frozen either. The bill also requires one-year minimum contracts in a digital registry and penalties for illegal increases. Tenants would provide a single guarantee instead of multiple co-signers, and a tenant ombudsman would give free legal defense. For the first time, the law recognizes gentrification as a process of social exclusion. About 30% of Mexico City families rent, and rents in the central boroughs have quintupled in 20 years.

🇲🇽⚖️ <u>Fake Government Websites Could Now Mean Prison</u>

Mexico's Chamber of Deputies voted 281 to 83 to reform the Federal Penal Code and the Industrial Property Law. Using, copying or imitating official government logos and symbols to commit fraud can now carry up to five years in prison. The target is criminal groups that build fake web pages dressed in government branding to charge people for procedures and payments. PRI, PAN and MC voted against and branded the bill the "Ley Antimemes", warning it could reach satire. The reform now goes to the Executive for publication in the DOF.
banner: FAKE GOV SITES: UP TO 5 YEARS

text:
🚨🇲🇽 <u>980,000 Deported Under Trump, 400,000 of Them Mexican</u>

The Trump administration deported more than 980,000 people between January 20, 2025 and July 31, 2026, according to the Migration Policy Institute, as reported by La Jornada. About 400,000 were Mexicans. Only 20% of those deported had a criminal conviction. 69% were caught at the border, and interior arrests are up 151%. Of the people ICE removed, 61% had lived in the US for at least two years, and 15% for a decade or more.
